chief_complaint: episodic irregular heartbeat, palpitations, and fatigue for 1 week
hpi_details: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with episodic irregular heartbeat, palpitations, and fatigue for 1 week. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks her palpitations and fatigue are due to an overactive thyroid or an early hormonal imbalance.
concerns: She is worried that her fluttering heart will cause a sudden stroke like the one that disabled her aunt.
expectations: She hopes to have an ECG done and leave with a prescription to keep her heart rhythm regular.

results.value: Atrial fibrillation with no discrete P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular rate of 126 bpm

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Atrial Fibrillation is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management requires ECG confirmation, assessment of haemodynamic stability, and individualized decisions on rate/rhythm control and anticoagulation based on thromboembolic risk rather than routine treatment for every patient.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: episodic irregular heartbeat, palpitations, and fatigue for 1 week

Key HPI features: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with episodic irregular heartbeat, palpitations, and fatigue for 1 week. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Atrial Fibrillation.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Atrial Fibrillation.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Atrial flutter without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any focal weakness, slurred speech, or visual loss — thromboembolism.
management_principles: Obtain ECG, assess haemodynamic stability, calculate CHA2DS2-VASc, and individualize rate/rhythm control and anticoagulation according to thromboembolic risk
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of episodic irregular heartbeat, palpitations, and fatigue for 1 week. HPI: ectopic atrial activity.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Atrial Fibrillation.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Atrial Fibrillation.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain ECG, assess haemodynamic stability, and calculate CHA2DS2-VASc. Individualize rate/rhythm control and anticoagulation according to thromboembolic risk; a 38-year-old woman without other risk factors does not routinely need anticoagulation.

teaching.one_liner: An irregularly irregular rhythm. Rate control, rhythm control and — above all — stroke prevention are the three decisions it forces.
red_flags: Any focal weakness, slurred speech, or visual loss — thromboembolism

must_ask.say: Does it come and go, or is it there all the time?
When you feel your pulse, is it irregular?
Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, heart failure, or a previous stroke?
Are you on any blood thinners, and have you ever had a serious bleed?
How much alcohol do you drink in a typical week?
How far can you walk on the flat before you need to stop?

history.answer: My heart has been beating irregularly and fluttering on and off for the past week, and I have been feeling unusually tired.
It feels like my heart is beating very fast and jumping all over the place, with chaotic and uneven thumps in my chest.
When it happens, the rhythm is totally erratic without any regular beat, just completely uneven and disorganized.
The fluttering starts fairly suddenly and tends to subside on its own after a while, rather than building up slowly.
It first started about a week ago, and each episode lasts from one to several hours and happens once or twice a day.
I have noticed it more when I am under stress at work or moving around, but sometimes it happens while I am just sitting down.
Resting quietly helps me feel a bit calmer, but holding my breath, bearing down, or drinking ice water has not stopped the fluttering.
I feel a bit short of breath and tired when I walk briskly or climb stairs during an episode, but I have not had any chest pain or pressure.
I felt lightheaded once or twice when the racing was fast, but I have never passed out or lost consciousness.
No, I have not had any facial drooping, arm weakness, numbness, speech difficulties, or sudden changes in my vision.
I have been feeling generalized fatigue and drained of energy all week, but I do not feel chronically dizzy.
No, I do not have heat intolerance, excessive sweating, unintended weight loss, or trembling in my hands.
No, I have not had unusually heavy periods, black tarry stools, easy bruising, or any abnormal bleeding.
No, I do not get severe pounding headaches, cold clammy sweats, sudden paleness, or shakiness before meals.
The fluttering makes me feel anxious when it starts, but I do not experience panic attacks, a sense of impending doom, or hyperventilating.
No, I have not had any recent fever, chills, sore throat, cough, or viral illness.
I drink one cup of brewed coffee in the morning and no energy drinks, which has been my usual routine for years.
I've been wondering if my thyroid is overactive or if my hormones are suddenly going haywire.
My aunt had an irregular heartbeat and ended up having a major stroke, so I'm terrified the exact same thing will happen to me.
I'm hoping to get an ECG done today and leave with some medicine to keep my heartbeat steady.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, or heart conditions.
I have never had high blood pressure, diabetes, vascular disease, or any previous strokes or mini-strokes.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I am not taking any prescription medicines, over-the-counter decongestants, cold remedies, diet pills, or herbal supplements.
I have never taken blood thinners or anticoagulants, and I have no bleeding disorders.
I do not have any known drug allergies.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
I only drink alcohol socially, perhaps one glass of wine or beer once a week or two, and I have not had any heavy drinking episodes recently.
I work as an office administrator and live with my husband; work has been moderately busy, but manageable.
There is no family history of heart arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, heart attacks at a young age, or sudden unexplained death.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago and my cycles are regular; I am not pregnant and we use barrier contraception.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable at rest, with normal breathing effort and no acute distress.
Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, pulse 126 beats/min and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Conjunctivae are pink with no pallor; sclerae are clear and non-icteric.
No exophthalmos, lid retraction, or lid lag noted; extraocular movements are full and intact.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, with no palpable nodules, goiter, or bruits.
No postural or resting fine tremor observed in the outstretched hands.
Irregularly irregular rhythm with variable S1 intensity, rate approximately 126 beats/min; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
Radial and pedal pulses are irregularly irregular with variable pulse volume and a rate matching heart auscultation at 126 beats/min.
Breath sounds are clear bilaterally with no crackles, wheezes, or ronchi.
Jugular venous pressure is normal at 2 cm above the sternal angle with no jugular venous distention.
No peripheral pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities; calves are non-tender and symmetrical.
